title: CLI design conventions
purpose: The rules the tools in bin/ follow, and the reasoning. Informed by the guidance at bettercli.org, narrowed to what a small single-purpose tool actually needs.
scope_note: Deliberately omitted for now: version flags, update checks, telemetry, config files, shell completions, subcommands. Each is a real cost and none is needed yet. Add one when a concrete need appears, not pre-emptively.

streams.rule: stdout is for requested data only. Everything else goes to stderr.
streams.why: This is what makes the tools pipeable. A single stray progress line on stdout corrupts a PPM stream, and the failure appears inside ffmpeg as an unrelated decode error.

success_and_silence.rule: Say nothing on success beyond a single confirmation line on stderr, suppressible with --quiet.
success_and_silence.why: Following cp and mv: a tool that succeeded has nothing to report. Output should be reserved for cases where the output IS the result.
success_and_silence.note: The confirmation goes to stderr, not stdout, so it never joins piped data.

progress.rule: Show progress only when stderr is an interactive terminal.
progress.implementation: isatty(fileno(stderr)) in the C++ runtime; [[ -t 2 ]] in bash.
progress.why: In a CI log or a redirected file, a carriage-return progress line becomes thousands of unreadable lines. Nobody is watching, so there is nothing to show.
progress.when: Only for work long enough to warrant it. Rendering qualifies; parsing arguments does not.

exit_codes.rationale: bettercli's advice is to stay binary (0/1) unless there is a real reason for more. The one distinction kept is usage error versus runtime failure, because a caller genuinely wants to treat them differently: a usage error means the command will never work and should not be retried, while a runtime failure may be transient.
exit_codes.nuance_belongs_in_stderr: Anything finer-grained than that goes in the message, not the code.

pipeline_caveat.problem: With `set -o pipefail`, a pipeline reports the rightmost failing command's status. When the renderer rejects an argument and exits 2, ffmpeg then fails on a truncated stream and its exit code (e.g. 234) masks the useful one.
pipeline_caveat.solution: Inspect PIPESTATUS and let the producer's status win, since it holds the real diagnosis.
pipeline_caveat.note: This was a live bug in this project's CLI, not a hypothetical.

rules: Name the tool, so the source is unambiguous in a pipeline.
State what was wrong with the input that was actually given, quoting it.
For an invalid choice, list the valid ones. `unknown parameter 'nope'` followed by `known parameters: octaves warp gain` turns a dead end into a fix.
On a usage error, point at --help rather than printing the whole help text.
No stack traces, no error codes to look up, no apologies.
errors.example:
plasma: unknown parameter 'nope'
  known parameters: octaves warp gain

conventions: Long flags are the primary interface; short flags only for the ones typed constantly (-o, -s, -j, -q, -h).
GNU-style double dashes. No single-dash long flags.
The primary required argument is positional -- `ppmr shaders/plasma.cpp` -- with --shader accepted as an explicit alias.
Repeatable flags for repeatable things: --set NAME=VALUE once per parameter, rather than a comma-separated list that then needs its own escaping rules.
Composite values only where they are conventionally written that way: --size 1920x1080 rather than --width and --height.
Optional flag arguments are avoided except where the default is obvious (--preview with no number means frame 0).
Every default is stated in --help. A default that has to be discovered by experiment is a bug.
naming: Name after intent, not mechanism: --samples, not --ssaa-grid-n.

rules: Fits on one screen. If it does not, the tool is doing too much.
Examples are the most-read section. Include the common case first, then two or three showing composition.
Help goes to stdout and exits 0 when requested with --help, because it was the requested output. Running with no arguments prints it to stderr and exits 2, because that was an error.
A shader binary's --help lists its own parameters with defaults and descriptions, generated from the Param declarations. The CLI needs no knowledge of any specific shader.

composability.rule: Each tool does one thing and hands off through a file or a pipe.
composability.shape: ppm-gen writes a shader file -> ppmr renders it. Neither needs to know the other exists.
composability.why: Generation and rendering fail for entirely different reasons and are used at different rates. Fusing them would mean re-running a network call to re-render at a different resolution.
composability.consequence: Both remain useful alone: hand-written shaders never touch ppm-gen, and a generated shader is an ordinary file that can be edited and committed.

caching.rule: Cache keys must cover every input that affects the output.
caching.implementation: The compile cache keys on the shader source, every header it may include, and the compiler command line.
caching.why: A cache keyed on the source alone serves a stale binary after a header change -- and the symptom is a wrong image, not an error, which is much worse.
caching.atomicity: Compile to a temporary name and rename on success, so an interrupted or failed build never leaves a broken binary that later looks like a cache hit.

rules: Never overwrite without being asked, except at an explicitly given --output path.
--dry-run prints the exact commands that would run, so a pipeline can be inspected or copied.
A generated shader is code that will be compiled and executed. ppm-gen writes it to a file and stops; it does not run it. Review before rendering.
